vignette:
The Weight of Hands

Elena is a 59-year-old Colombian-born physical therapist who has spent the better part of three decades helping people recover the use of their bodies. She is precise, warm, and deeply attentive to her patients — qualities that seem to emerge from somewhere older and more complicated than professional training. She has been divorced for eleven years and lives alone in a tidy apartment she describes as "finally mine." She came to therapy, she says, because her body has started refusing to cooperate with the life she has built.

Growing up in Medellín, Elena was the eldest of four children in a household governed by her father's moods. He was a man who could be charming and generous in public, and who could, without warning, become something else entirely at home. The beatings were not random — they followed a logic she spent years trying to decode, believing that if she understood the pattern, she could prevent them. She learned to read the tightness around his jaw, the particular way he set down a glass. She became, as she puts it, "an expert in other people's bodies before I ever studied anatomy." Her mother did not intervene. This, Elena says quietly, was its own kind of wound.

She left for Bogotá at eighteen, then eventually emigrated to the United States for graduate school. She built her career methodically, married, had a son who is now grown, and divorced a husband she describes as "not cruel, just absent." For many years she functioned well — or believed she did. She kept busy. Busyness, she has come to understand, was a strategy.

The unraveling began two years ago when a patient — a large man recovering from a shoulder injury — lost his temper during a session and slammed his fist against the treatment table inches from her hand. He was not targeting her. He was frustrated with his own body. But something in Elena shut down and then flooded open simultaneously. She finished the session. She drove home. She sat in her car in the parking garage for two hours, unable to move, certain that something terrible was about to happen, though she could not name what.

Since then, she startles at sounds she previously ignored — a door closing too hard, a voice raised in the hallway. She finds herself scanning her patients' faces for signs of anger, tracking their hands even when she is supposed to be focused on their range of motion. Some nights she wakes at three in the morning with her heart slamming, pulled out of dreams she cannot fully remember but that leave the taste of her childhood kitchen in her mouth. She lies awake cataloguing small failures, convinced she has missed something important, that something is her fault.

She has begun avoiding male patients when she can arrange it, a fact that troubles her professionally and that she has told no one at work. She rearranges her schedule under the guise of "caseload management." She is meticulous about this deception, which exhausts her.

What she finds most disorienting is the way her hands — the instruments of her profession, the tools she has always trusted — sometimes feel foreign to her during treatment sessions. She will be performing a mobilization she has done ten thousand times and suddenly become aware of her own hands as if from a distance, as if they belong to someone else. She knows the clinical term for this. Knowing the term does not make it stop.

She describes her interior life as "a house with a room I keep locked." She has been successful, she says, at keeping it locked. What frightens her now is that the lock seems to be getting old. She is 59 years old, she says, and she is tired of standing guard.

She wants, she tells her therapist in their third session, to stop being afraid of men who are simply in pain. She wants to stop flinching. She says this matter-of-factly, as though it is a modest request. Her eyes say otherwise.
